claim: The Triaka point mutation results in a methionine-to-valine substitution at amino acid position 161 (M161V) of ESRP1.
source: The Triaka point mutation results in a methionine-to-valine substitution at the amino acid position 161 (M161V) of ESRP1, a residue conserved in several species (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the specific mutation and its location, with reference to a figure showing conservation.

claim: The M161V residue of ESRP1 is conserved in several species.
source: The Triaka point mutation results in a methionine-to-valine substitution at the amino acid position 161 (M161V) of ESRP1, a residue conserved in several species (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The text states conservation across species, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1 shows alignment data demonstrating this conservation.

claim: Triaka animals develop overtly normal.
source: Triaka animals develop overtly normal (see also Materials and methods), which allows investigation of the physiological role of Esrp1 in adults.
evidence: Direct observation of animal development reported in the manuscript.

claim: Esrp1-/- mice are neonatal lethal.
source: This is in contrast to the recently published Esrp1-/- or skin epithelial-specific Esrp1-deficient animals that are neonatal lethal (Bebee et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study (Bebee et al., 2015) reporting neonatal lethality.

claim: WT ESRP1 protein led to a 2.4-fold increase of Cd44v5 inclusion compared to control.
source: We found that WT ESRP1 protein led to a 2.4 and 10.9 fold increase of Cd44 variable exon v5 (Cd44v5) and Fgfr2 variable exon IIIb (Fgfr2-IIIb) inclusion, respectively, compared to control.
evidence: Quantitative measurement from in vitro reporter assay shown in Figure 1A.

claim: WT ESRP1 protein led to a 10.9-fold increase of Fgfr2-IIIb inclusion compared to control.
source: We found that WT ESRP1 protein led to a 2.4 and 10.9 fold increase of Cd44 variable exon v5 (Cd44v5) and Fgfr2 variable exon IIIb (Fgfr2-IIIb) inclusion, respectively, compared to control.
evidence: Quantitative measurement from in vitro reporter assay shown in Figure 1B.

claim: ESRP1Triaka showed 1.8-fold induction of Cd44v5 inclusion.
source: ESRP1Triaka however showed reduced levels of Cd44v5 and Fgfr2-IIIb inclusion, with 1.8 and 3.3 fold induction, respectively (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from in vitro reporter assay shown in Figure 1A.

claim: ESRP1Triaka showed 3.3-fold induction of Fgfr2-IIIb inclusion.
source: ESRP1Triaka however showed reduced levels of Cd44v5 and Fgfr2-IIIb inclusion, with 1.8 and 3.3 fold induction, respectively (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from in vitro reporter assay shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Esrp1-regulated splicing events show distinct sensitivity to Esrp1 loss.
source: This variation in the extent of in vitro splicing of Cd44 versus Fgfr2 by ESRP1Triaka likely related to the fact that Esrp1-regulated splicing events show distinct sensitivity to Esrp1 loss (Warzecha et al., 2009; Bebee et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites two studies (Warzecha et al., 2009; Bebee et al., 2015) that reported differential sensitivity.

claim: Esrp1Triaka led to diminished inclusion of Cd44v4/5 in CMT-93 cells compared to Esrp1WT at the same level of overexpression.
source: At the same level of overexpression as Esrp1WT, Esrp1Triaka led to diminished inclusion of Cd44v4/5 in CMT-93 cells and reduced cell proliferation (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: Experimental data from CMT-93 cells shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: Esrp1Triaka reduced cell proliferation in CMT-93 cells compared to Esrp1WT at the same level of overexpression.
source: At the same level of overexpression as Esrp1WT, Esrp1Triaka led to diminished inclusion of Cd44v4/5 in CMT-93 cells and reduced cell proliferation (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: Experimental data from CMT-93 cells shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: Esrp1WT transcript levels directly correlated with frequency of Cd44v4/5 splicing events.
source: Of note, Esrp1WT transcript levels directly correlated with frequency of Cd44v4/5 splicing events, suggesting a dose-dependent effect of Esrp1 expression on Esrp1-mediated splicing activity (Figure 1F).
evidence: Correlation analysis shown in Figure 1F demonstrates the relationship between transcript levels and splicing frequency.

claim: Esrp1 expression has a dose-dependent effect on Esrp1-mediated splicing activity.
source: Of note, Esrp1WT transcript levels directly correlated with frequency of Cd44v4/5 splicing events, suggesting a dose-dependent effect of Esrp1 expression on Esrp1-mediated splicing activity (Figure 1F).
evidence: The correlation data in Figure 1F supports this inference about dose-dependency.

claim: Esrp1Triaka reduces ESRP1 function.
source: Taken together, these in vitro data indicate that Esrp1Triaka reduces ESRP1 function, and thereby decreases the proliferative capacity of epithelial cells.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on multiple in vitro experiments (Figure 1A-F).

claim: Esrp1Triaka decreases the proliferative capacity of epithelial cells.
source: Taken together, these in vitro data indicate that Esrp1Triaka reduces ESRP1 function, and thereby decreases the proliferative capacity of epithelial cells.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on proliferation assays shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Esrp1 is highly expressed in the murine large intestine.
source: Esrp1 has been shown to be epithelial cell-restricted and to be highly expressed in the murine large intestine (Warzecha et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study (Warzecha et al., 2009) reporting high expression in large intestine.

claim: Esrp1 is epithelial cell-restricted.
source: Esrp1 has been shown to be epithelial cell-restricted and to be highly expressed in the murine large intestine (Warzecha et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study (Warzecha et al., 2009) reporting epithelial cell restriction.

claim: 35 genes showed different relative frequency of splicing isoforms in Esrp1Triaka versus Esrp1WT cIECs.
source: Computational analysis revealed 35 genes for which the relative frequency of splicing isoforms differed in Esrp1Triaka versus Esrp1WT cIECs (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: RNA sequencing analysis results shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Cd44 is a previously reported ESRP1 target gene.
source: These findings were validated using quantitative reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) for selected, previously reported ESRP1 target genes, including Cd44 and Magi1 (Brown et al., 2011; Warzecha et al., 2009; Warzecha et al., 2010), and for novel candidate targets, including Uap1 and Gpr137 (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript cites published studies (Brown et al., 2011; Warzecha et al., 2009; Warzecha et al., 2010) that previously identified Cd44 as an ESRP1 target.

claim: Magi1 is a previously reported ESRP1 target gene.
source: These findings were validated using quantitative reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) for selected, previously reported ESRP1 target genes, including Cd44 and Magi1 (Brown et al., 2011; Warzecha et al., 2009; Warzecha et al., 2010), and for novel candidate targets, including Uap1 and Gpr137 (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript cites published studies (Brown et al., 2011; Warzecha et al., 2009; Warzecha et al., 2010) that previously identified Magi1 as an ESRP1 target.

claim: Uap1 is a novel candidate ESRP1 target gene.
source: These findings were validated using quantitative reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) for selected, previously reported ESRP1 target genes, including Cd44 and Magi1 (Brown et al., 2011; Warzecha et al., 2009; Warzecha et al., 2010), and for novel candidate targets, including Uap1 and Gpr137 (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript identifies Uap1 as a novel target based on RNA sequencing analysis.

claim: Gpr137 is a novel candidate ESRP1 target gene.
source: These findings were validated using quantitative reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) for selected, previously reported ESRP1 target genes, including Cd44 and Magi1 (Brown et al., 2011; Warzecha et al., 2009; Warzecha et al., 2010), and for novel candidate targets, including Uap1 and Gpr137 (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript identifies Gpr137 as a novel target based on RNA sequencing analysis.

claim: Expression of CD44v4-containing isoforms was reduced in colonic sections of Triaka versus WT mice.
source: Functional alterations induced by ESRP1Triaka were also apparent on the protein level, as expression of CD44 variant 4 (CD44v4)-containing isoforms, but not total CD44, was reduced in colonic sections of Triaka versus WT mice (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Total CD44 expression was not reduced in colonic sections of Triaka versus WT mice.
source: Functional alterations induced by ESRP1Triaka were also apparent on the protein level, as expression of CD44 variant 4 (CD44v4)-containing isoforms, but not total CD44, was reduced in colonic sections of Triaka versus WT mice (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Several pathways involved in cell cycle and proliferation were affected in Triaka cIECs.
source: Pathway analysis of the RNA sequencing data showed that several pathways involved in cell cycle and proliferation were affected in Triaka cIECs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Gene set enrichment analysis results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Crypt depth was similar in Triaka versus WT mice.
source: Yet, these transcriptional changes did not overtly alter intestinal histomorphology and epithelial proliferation, as crypt depth, number of goblet cells and Ki-67 expression were similar in Triaka versus WT mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–F).
evidence: Histological measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-F.

claim: Number of goblet cells was similar in Triaka versus WT mice.
source: Yet, these transcriptional changes did not overtly alter intestinal histomorphology and epithelial proliferation, as crypt depth, number of goblet cells and Ki-67 expression were similar in Triaka versus WT mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–F).
evidence: Histological measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-F.

claim: Ki-67 expression was similar in Triaka versus WT mice at steady-state.
source: Yet, these transcriptional changes did not overtly alter intestinal histomorphology and epithelial proliferation, as crypt depth, number of goblet cells and Ki-67 expression were similar in Triaka versus WT mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–F).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-F.

claim: Triaka and WT mice showed similar colon length at steady-state.
source: Furthermore, Triaka and WT mice showed similar colon length at steady-state (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: Colon length measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2G.

claim: E-cadherin (CDH1) surface expression was reduced on Triaka cIECs.
source: However, E-cadherin (CDH1) surface expression was reduced on Triaka cIECs (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Triaka colonic mucosa showed increased ion permeability compared to WT.
source: Indeed, ex vivo measurement of the intestinal electrical resistance indicated an increased ion permeability of Triaka versus WT colonic mucosa (Figure 3C), although there was no such difference in the small intestine (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Ussing chamber measurements shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There was no difference in ion permeability between Triaka and WT small intestine.
source: Indeed, ex vivo measurement of the intestinal electrical resistance indicated an increased ion permeability of Triaka versus WT colonic mucosa (Figure 3C), although there was no such difference in the small intestine (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Ussing chamber measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Bacterial 16S rRNA was present in intestinal crypts and inner mucus layer of Triaka but not WT colons.
source: This was accompanied by the presence of bacterial 16S rRNA in intestinal crypts and in the inner mucus layer of Triaka but not WT colons (Figure 3D and Table 1).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3D and quantified in Table 1.

claim: Systemic anti-commensal IgG1 antibody reactivity was detected in most Triaka mice but rarely in control animals.
source: As further indirect evidence of reduced barrier integrity, we also detected systemic anti-commensal IgG1 and IgG2b antibody reactivity towards autologous intestinal bacteria in most Triaka mice, but rarely in control animals (Figure 3E and Table 1).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3E and quantified in Table 1.

claim: Systemic anti-commensal IgG2b antibody reactivity was detected in most Triaka mice but rarely in control animals.
source: As further indirect evidence of reduced barrier integrity, we also detected systemic anti-commensal IgG1 and IgG2b antibody reactivity towards autologous intestinal bacteria in most Triaka mice, but rarely in control animals (Figure 3E and Table 1).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3E and quantified in Table 1.

claim: Levels of fecal albumin were similar in fecal pellets of Triaka and WT mice.
source: However, levels of fecal albumin and lipocalin-2 – markers for intestinal lesions and inflammation – were similar in fecal pellets of Triaka and WT mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B and C).
evidence: ELISA measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B and C.

claim: Levels of fecal lipocalin-2 were similar in fecal pellets of Triaka and WT mice.
source: However, levels of fecal albumin and lipocalin-2 – markers for intestinal lesions and inflammation – were similar in fecal pellets of Triaka and WT mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B and C).
evidence: ELISA measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B and C.

claim: There was no difference in the resorption of macromolecules between Triaka and WT mice.
source: Furthermore, there was no difference in the resorption of macromolecules between Triaka and WT mice (22 ± 1 versus 24 ± 3 µg/ml serum FITC-dextran-4000 levels, respectively, p=0.6).
evidence: FITC-dextran permeability assay results reported in the text.

claim: Triaka mice showed increased weight loss compared to WT controls after DSS treatment.
source: Compared with WT controls, Triaka animals treated with dextran sodium sulfate (DSS) in drinking water for 7 days, a disease model of intestinal inflammation and damage, showed increased weight loss and pronounced shortening of the colon (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Weight loss measurements shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Triaka mice showed pronounced shortening of the colon compared to WT controls after DSS treatment.
source: Compared with WT controls, Triaka animals treated with dextran sodium sulfate (DSS) in drinking water for 7 days, a disease model of intestinal inflammation and damage, showed increased weight loss and pronounced shortening of the colon (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Colon length measurements shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Triaka mice showed higher disease scores, both clinically and histologically, after DSS treatment.
source: This was also reflected by higher disease scores, both clinically and histologically (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Disease scoring data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The DSS phenotype was not due to an altered drinking behavior of Triaka animals.
source: Notably, this phenotype was not due to an altered drinking behavior of Triaka animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Water consumption measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Triaka mice were more susceptible to chronic DSS-induced colitis.
source: In addition, Triaka mice were also more susceptible to chronic DSS-induced colitis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Chronic DSS colitis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Triaka mice showed diminished wound-healing compared with WT mice in an in vivo wound-healing model.
source: In these settings, we observed diminished wound-healing in Triaka compared with WT mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: Colonoscopy-based wound-healing measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Esrp1Triaka impairs the proliferative or regenerative capacity of cIECs during intestinal pathology.
source: In contrast to what we observed at steady-state, these data imply that Esrp1Triaka impairs the proliferative or regenerative capacity of cIECs during intestinal pathology.
evidence: Inference based on wound-healing data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Colorectal tumors were reduced in number in AOM/DSS-treated Triaka mice compared with WT controls.
source: We found that in azoxymethane (AOM) and DSS-treated Triaka mice, colorectal tumors were reduced in number and size compared with WT controls, thus providing additional evidence for a defective proliferation of Triaka IECs (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: Tumor count data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Colorectal tumors were reduced in size in AOM/DSS-treated Triaka mice compared with WT controls.
source: We found that in azoxymethane (AOM) and DSS-treated Triaka mice, colorectal tumors were reduced in number and size compared with WT controls, thus providing additional evidence for a defective proliferation of Triaka IECs (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: Tumor size measurements shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The tumor grade was not different between Triaka and WT mice in the AOM/DSS model.
source: The tumor grade was not different between the two groups (Figure 4F).
evidence: Tumor grading data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Matrix metalloproteinase-3 was more upregulated in Triaka versus WT tumors.
source: However, molecular analysis revealed more pronounced upregulation of matrix metalloproteinase-3, granulocyte-colony stimulating factor, transforming growth factor β1 and interleukin-1α in Triaka versus WT tumors (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Cytokine measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Granulocyte-colony stimulating factor was more upregulated in Triaka versus WT tumors.
source: However, molecular analysis revealed more pronounced upregulation of matrix metalloproteinase-3, granulocyte-colony stimulating factor, transforming growth factor β1 and interleukin-1α in Triaka versus WT tumors (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Cytokine measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Transforming growth factor β1 was more upregulated in Triaka versus WT tumors.
source: However, molecular analysis revealed more pronounced upregulation of matrix metalloproteinase-3, granulocyte-colony stimulating factor, transforming growth factor β1 and interleukin-1α in Triaka versus WT tumors (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Cytokine measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Interleukin-1α was more upregulated in Triaka versus WT tumors.
source: However, molecular analysis revealed more pronounced upregulation of matrix metalloproteinase-3, granulocyte-colony stimulating factor, transforming growth factor β1 and interleukin-1α in Triaka versus WT tumors (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Cytokine measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Matrix metalloproteinase-3, granulocyte-colony stimulating factor, transforming growth factor β1 and interleukin-1α are established drivers of CRC progression, EMT and metastasis.
source: These proteins are all established drivers of CRC progression, EMT and metastasis, thus indicating a more aggressive phenotype of Triaka tumors (Li et al., 2016; Mroczko et al., 2006; Morris et al., 2014; Calon et al., 2012; Matsuo et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple published studies (Li et al., 2016; Mroczko et al., 2006; Morris et al., 2014; Calon et al., 2012; Matsuo et al., 2009) that established these proteins as drivers of CRC progression.

claim: Triaka cIECs expressed a partial EMT signature prior to transformation.
source: These features of Esrp1Triaka CRC lesions likely resulted from a partial EMT signature expressed by Triaka cIECs, prior to transformation (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Gene expression data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Triaka cIECs showed reduced Ki-67 expression compared with WT cIECs after 3 days of DSS treatment.
source: Under these conditions of mild intestinal inflammation, which are not sufficient to induce epithelial erosions, Triaka cIECs showed reduced Ki-67 expression compared with WT cIECs (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: Altered Esrp1-regulated mRNA splicing deregulates cIEC function and affects the development of intestinal disease in Triaka mice through a mechanism reducing IEC proliferation.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that altered Esrp1-regulated mRNA splicing deregulates cIEC function and affects the development of intestinal disease in Triaka mice, through a mechanism reducing IEC proliferation.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on multiple disease model experiments (Figure 4).

claim: Gpr137 is involved in IEC proliferation.
source: Of those, Gpr137 emerged as a prominent candidate since it is involved in IEC proliferation (Zhang et al., 2014), although the mode of action of this orphan G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) or of its isoforms is unknown.
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study (Zhang et al., 2014) that reported Gpr137's involvement in IEC proliferation.

claim: The mode of action of GPR137 or its isoforms is unknown.
source: Of those, Gpr137 emerged as a prominent candidate since it is involved in IEC proliferation (Zhang et al., 2014), although the mode of action of this orphan G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) or of its isoforms is unknown.
evidence: The manuscript states that the mechanism is unknown, indicating a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Gpr137_Long is preferentially expressed in Triaka cIECs.
source: Our RNA sequencing analysis indicated that Gpr137_Long is preferentially expressed in Triaka cIECs, whereas Gpr137_Short is predominant in WT cIECs.
evidence: RNA sequencing analysis results reported in the text and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Gpr137_Short is predominant in WT cIECs.
source: Our RNA sequencing analysis indicated that Gpr137_Long is preferentially expressed in Triaka cIECs, whereas Gpr137_Short is predominant in WT cIECs.
evidence: RNA sequencing analysis results reported in the text and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Gpr137 is a splicing target of ESRP1.
source: By using our in vitro reporter system, we could validate that Gpr137 is a splicing target of ESRP1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: In vitro reporter assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Gpr137_Long-expressing cells showed decreased cell proliferation compared to Gpr137_Short-expressing cells.
source: We found a decreased cell proliferation and diminished epithelial monolayer tightness, as indicated by lower electrical resistance, in Gpr137_Long- versus Gpr137_Short-expressing cells.
evidence: Cell proliferation assays shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Gpr137_Long-expressing cells showed diminished epithelial monolayer tightness compared to Gpr137_Short-expressing cells.
source: We found a decreased cell proliferation and diminished epithelial monolayer tightness, as indicated by lower electrical resistance, in Gpr137_Long- versus Gpr137_Short-expressing cells.
evidence: TEER measurements shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The barrier function appeared to be distinct from IEC proliferation in the epithelial monolayer assay.
source: Importantly, in this particular assay the barrier function appeared to be distinct from the IEC proliferation. Indeed, although control vector-transduced cells proliferated less than cells transduced with vectors encoding Gpr137 isoforms, they formed a tighter barrier (Figure 5A and B, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Comparison of proliferation and TEER data shown in Figure 5A, B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The effects of the two Gpr137 isoforms on IEC proliferation and barrier integrity were independent of their relative expression levels.
source: These effects of the two Gpr137 isoforms on IEC proliferation and barrier integrity were independent of their relative expression levels and of possible cytotoxic effects (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: Expression level and cytotoxicity data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: The effects of the two Gpr137 isoforms on IEC proliferation and barrier integrity were independent of possible cytotoxic effects.
source: These effects of the two Gpr137 isoforms on IEC proliferation and barrier integrity were independent of their relative expression levels and of possible cytotoxic effects (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: Cytotoxicity data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Transduction with Gpr137 isoforms distinctively enhanced the proliferation of murine MC-38 IEC lines.
source: Transduction with Gpr137 isoforms also distinctively enhanced the proliferation of murine MC-38 and human Caco-2 IEC lines, thus validating our findings in CMT-93 cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: Proliferation assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Transduction with Gpr137 isoforms distinctively enhanced the proliferation of human Caco-2 IEC lines.
source: Transduction with Gpr137 isoforms also distinctively enhanced the proliferation of murine MC-38 and human Caco-2 IEC lines, thus validating our findings in CMT-93 cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: Proliferation assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2E.

claim: There was a one-third reduction in levels of active β-catenin protein in Gpr137_Long- versus Gpr137_Short-transduced cells.
source: Indeed, we found a one-third reduction in levels of active β-catenin protein in Gpr137_Long- versus Gpr137_Short-transduced cells (Figure 5C), which was validated in Esrp1Triaka- versus Esrp1WT-transduced cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of Wnt/β-catenin signaling abrogated the proliferative advantage of Gpr137_Short- over Gpr137_Long-transduced cells.
source: Furthermore, pharmacological inhibition of Wnt/β-catenin signaling abrogated the proliferative advantage of Gpr137_Short- over Gpr137_Long-transduced cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: Proliferation assay with XAV-939 inhibitor shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Gpr137 isoforms modify epithelial function via regulation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling.
source: This suggested that Gpr137 isoforms modify epithelial function via regulation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling.
evidence: Inference based on active β-catenin measurements and inhibitor experiments shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: cIECs of Triaka mice showed ca. 40% reduced levels of active β-catenin compared with WT mice.
source: In line with these in vitro data, we measured ca. 40% reduced levels of active β-catenin, as well as diminished expression of Wnt target genes (Herbst et al., 2014) in cIECs of Triaka compared with WT mice (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: cIECs of Triaka mice showed diminished expression of Wnt target genes compared with WT mice.
source: In line with these in vitro data, we measured ca. 40% reduced levels of active β-catenin, as well as diminished expression of Wnt target genes (Herbst et al., 2014) in cIECs of Triaka compared with WT mice (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: qPCR data shown in Figure 5F, with Wnt target genes identified by Herbst et al., 2014.

claim: Distinct Gpr137 isoforms can differently modulate the Wnt/β-catenin pathway and IEC function.
source: Collectively, these results show that distinct Gpr137 isoforms can differently modulate the Wnt/β-catenin pathway and IEC function, which may partially underlie the intestinal phenotype of Triaka mice.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on multiple experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: ESRP1 levels were downregulated in inflamed biopsies from CD intestines compared with non-inflamed paired biopsies.
source: Compared with non-inflamed paired biopsies, ESRP1 levels were downregulated in the inflamed biopsies from CD intestines (Figure 6A).
evidence: qPCR data from CD patient biopsies shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Nuclear ESRP1 expression was reduced in the inflamed CD intestine.
source: This correlated with reduced nuclear ESRP1 expression in the inflamed CD intestine, as measured by high-throughput automated immunohistochemistry quantification (Figure 6B).
evidence: Automated IHC quantification data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: ESRP1 protein is gradually downregulated during the adenoma to carcinoma sequence in intestinal tumors.
source: A tissue microarray (TMA) based analysis of matched intestinal tissues from a cohort of 185 CRC patients, which revealed a gradual decrease in nuclear expression of ESRP1 protein during cancer progression (Table 2).
evidence: TMA analysis data shown in Table 2.

claim: Low nuclear ESRP1 expression was associated with reduced patient survival.
source: Furthermore, low nuclear ESRP1 expression was associated with reduced patient survival (p=0.0456), larger tumors (p=0.0034), lymphatic invasion (p=0.0466), advanced pT-stage (p=0.02) and presence of nodal metastasis (p=0.016) (Figure 6C and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Survival analysis and clinicopathological correlation data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—source data 1.

claim: Low nuclear ESRP1 expression was associated with larger tumors.
source: Furthermore, low nuclear ESRP1 expression was associated with reduced patient survival (p=0.0456), larger tumors (p=0.0034), lymphatic invasion (p=0.0466), advanced pT-stage (p=0.02) and presence of nodal metastasis (p=0.016) (Figure 6C and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Clinicopathological correlation data shown in Figure 6—source data 1.

claim: Low nuclear ESRP1 expression was associated with lymphatic invasion.
source: Furthermore, low nuclear ESRP1 expression was associated with reduced patient survival (p=0.0456), larger tumors (p=0.0034), lymphatic invasion (p=0.0466), advanced pT-stage (p=0.02) and presence of nodal metastasis (p=0.016) (Figure 6C and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Clinicopathological correlation data shown in Figure 6—source data 1.

claim: Low nuclear ESRP1 expression was associated with advanced pT-stage.
source: Furthermore, low nuclear ESRP1 expression was associated with reduced patient survival (p=0.0456), larger tumors (p=0.0034), lymphatic invasion (p=0.0466), advanced pT-stage (p=0.02) and presence of nodal metastasis (p=0.016) (Figure 6C and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Clinicopathological correlation data shown in Figure 6—source data 1.

claim: Low nuclear ESRP1 expression was associated with presence of nodal metastasis.
source: Furthermore, low nuclear ESRP1 expression was associated with reduced patient survival (p=0.0456), larger tumors (p=0.0034), lymphatic invasion (p=0.0466), advanced pT-stage (p=0.02) and presence of nodal metastasis (p=0.016) (Figure 6C and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Clinicopathological correlation data shown in Figure 6—source data 1.

claim: ESRP1 expression was determined to be an independent prognostic factor in CRC.
source: ESRP1 expression was determined to be an independent prognostic factor, after adjusting for the confounding effects of pT, pN, pM, tumor budding, and lymphatic invasion (Figure 6—source data 2).
evidence: Multivariate survival analysis shown in Figure 6—source data 2.

claim: There was a positive correlation between the expression of ESRP1 and hGPR137_Short in normal intestine tissue.
source: We found a positive correlation between the expression of ESRP1 and GPR137_ENST00000539833 (referred hereafter as hGPR137_Short) in normal intestine tissue, which we further validated using independent samples (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Correlation analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 6D and validated in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There was an association between hGPR137_Short expression and transcript levels of Wnt target genes.
source: Moreover, there was an association between hGPR137_Short expression and transcript levels of Wnt target genes, suggesting a similar signaling downstream of GPR137 in humans and mice (Figure 6—source data 3).
evidence: Correlation analysis shown in Figure 6—source data 3.

claim: The ratio between hGPR137_Short and hGPR137_Long isoforms was altered in human CRC compared with normal intestinal tissue.
source: In human CRC, the ratio between hGPR137_Short and GPR137_ENST00000377702 (referred hereafter as hGPR137_Long) isoforms was altered compared with normal intestinal tissue (Figure 6E).
evidence: TCGA RNA sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Transcript levels of Gpr137_Long were increased in murine CRC tissue.
source: Similarly, transcript levels of Gpr137_Long were increased in murine CRC tissue (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: qPCR data from AOM/DSS-treated mice shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A higher ratio of hGPR137_Short to hGPR137_Long transcripts predicted enhanced CRC patient survival.
source: Importantly, a higher ratio of hGPR137_Short to hGPR137_Long transcripts predicted enhanced CRC patient survival, thereby indicating a protective role of the ESRP1-dependent hGPR137_Short isoform (Figure 6F).
evidence: Survival analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Higher expression levels of hGPR137_Short alone was associated with better prognosis in CRC.
source: Indeed, higher expression levels of hGPR137_Short alone was also associated with better prognosis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).

claim: Downregulation or loss of ESRP1 function results in dysregulation of alternative mRNA splicing in IECs.
source: Collectively, our data in mice and humans indicate that downregulation or loss of ESRP1 function results in dysregulation of alternative mRNA splicing in IECs.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on data from both mouse and human studies throughout the manuscript.

claim: Downregulation or loss of ESRP1 function leads to impaired epithelial cell integrity.
source: Collectively, our data in mice and humans indicate that downregulation or loss of ESRP1 function results in dysregulation of alternative mRNA splicing in IECs. This leads to impaired epithelial cell integrity and contributes to intestinal pathology, possibly via altered Gpr137/GPR137 isoform ratios (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Summary conclusion based on barrier integrity and disease model data shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: Downregulation or loss of ESRP1 function contributes to intestinal pathology, possibly via altered Gpr137/GPR137 isoform ratios.
source: Collectively, our data in mice and humans indicate that downregulation or loss of ESRP1 function results in dysregulation of alternative mRNA splicing in IECs. This leads to impaired epithelial cell integrity and contributes to intestinal pathology, possibly via altered Gpr137/GPR137 isoform ratios (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Summary conclusion based on mechanistic studies shown in Figure 5 and disease models shown in Figure 4.

claim: Alternative splicing of pre-mRNAs is estimated to occur in 92–94% of human genes.
source: Alternative splicing of pre-mRNAs (AS) is a common posttranscriptional modification that is estimated to occur in 92–94% of human genes (Wang et al., 2008; Pan et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites published studies (Wang et al., 2008; Pan et al., 2008) that estimated this frequency.

claim: AS permits generation of protein isoforms with related, distinct or sometimes even opposing functions.
source: AS permits generation of protein isoforms with related, distinct or sometimes even opposing functions (Vorlová et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study (Vorlová et al., 2011) that described this property of AS.

claim: Certain isoforms influence cancer progression.
source: Moreover, certain isoforms influence cancer progression (Brown et al., 2011) or are associated with autoimmune and inflammatory disorders (Ueda et al., 2003; Laitinen et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study (Brown et al., 2011) that showed isoforms influence cancer progression.

claim: Certain isoforms are associated with autoimmune and inflammatory disorders.
source: Moreover, certain isoforms influence cancer progression (Brown et al., 2011) or are associated with autoimmune and inflammatory disorders (Ueda et al., 2003; Laitinen et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites published studies (Ueda et al., 2003; Laitinen et al., 2004) that showed associations with autoimmune and inflammatory disorders.

claim: Alterations of mRNA splicing have been reported in human colorectal cancer.
source: While alterations of mRNA splicing have been reported in human colorectal cancer (CRC) (Freund et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2014) and IBD (Häsler et al., 2011; Mailer et al., 2015), the consequences of deregulated AS for intestinal homeostasis and disease development are largely unexplored.
evidence: The manuscript cites published studies (Freund et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2014) that reported splicing alterations in CRC.

claim: Alterations of mRNA splicing have been reported in IBD.
source: While alterations of mRNA splicing have been reported in human colorectal cancer (CRC) (Freund et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2014) and IBD (Häsler et al., 2011; Mailer et al., 2015), the consequences of deregulated AS for intestinal homeostasis and disease development are largely unexplored.
evidence: The manuscript cites published studies (Häsler et al., 2011; Mailer et al., 2015) that reported splicing alterations in IBD.

claim: ESRP1 was identified in a cDNA expression screen for factors that promote the epithelial pattern of FGFR2 splicing.
source: Epithelial splicing regulatory protein 1 (ESRP1), which is exclusively expressed in epithelial cells, was identified in a cDNA expression screen for factors that promote the epithelial pattern of FGFR2 (Fibroblast Growth Factor Receptor 2) splicing.
evidence: The manuscript describes how ESRP1 was originally identified, drawing from established knowledge.

claim: ESRP1 was found to regulate the AS of CD44 and other genes.
source: ESRP1 was also found to regulate the AS of CD44 and other genes (Warzecha et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study (Warzecha et al., 2009) that identified CD44 as an ESRP1 target.

claim: ESRP1 is negatively regulated by mesenchymal transcription factors such as SNAIL, ZEB1 and ZEB2.
source: ESRP1 is negatively regulated by mesenchymal transcription factors such as SNAIL, ZEB1 and ZEB2 (Preca et al., 2015; Saitoh, 2015; Reinke et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites published studies (Preca et al., 2015; Saitoh, 2015; Reinke et al., 2012) that showed negative regulation by these transcription factors.

claim: ESRP1 acts as a tumor suppressor by negatively regulating epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and the metastatic potential of human breast cancer cell lines.
source: Recently, ESRP1 has been reported to act as a tumor suppressor by negatively regulating epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and the metastatic potential of human breast cancer cell lines, via the splicing of different isoforms of CD44 or EXO70 (Lu et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study (Lu et al., 2013) that reported this tumor suppressor function.

claim: ESRP1 can suppress cancer cell motility in head and neck carcinoma cell lines.
source: ESRP1 can suppress cancer cell motility in head and neck carcinoma cell lines (Ishii et al., 2014) and ESRP1 protein expression is a favorable prognostic factor in pancreatic cancer (Ueda et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study (Ishii et al., 2014) that showed suppression of cancer cell motility.

claim: ESRP1 protein expression is a favorable prognostic factor in pancreatic cancer.
source: ESRP1 can suppress cancer cell motility in head and neck carcinoma cell lines (Ishii et al., 2014) and ESRP1 protein expression is a favorable prognostic factor in pancreatic cancer (Ueda et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study (Ueda et al., 2014) that showed favorable prognosis association.

claim: ESRP1 may promote lung metastasis of orthotopically transplanted breast cancer cells by generating CD44 isoforms independently of EMT.
source: However, ESRP1 may also promote lung metastasis of orthotopically transplanted breast cancer cells by generating CD44 isoforms independently of EMT (Yae et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study (Yae et al., 2012) that showed this pro-metastatic function.

claim: The lack of viable animal models has precluded analyzing the role of ESRP1-mediated AS for intestinal disease in vivo.
source: Yet, the contribution of ESRP1 to intestinal integrity and function is poorly investigated. Importantly, the lack of viable animal models so far has precluded analyzing the role of ESRP1-mediated AS for intestinal disease in vivo.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a gap in the field that their work addresses.

claim: The Triaka mutation was mapped to proximal Chromosome 4, with a peak LOD score of 2.71 at D4Mit235.
source: (A) The Triaka mutation was mapped based on the hyperactivity and circling phenotype of the strain to proximal Chromosome 4, with a peak LOD score of 2.71 at D4Mit235.
evidence: Genetic mapping data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: GPR137 is ubiquitously and abundantly expressed in mouse tissues.
source: GPR137 is ubiquitously and abundantly expressed in mouse tissues and is most closely related to OR51E2/PSGR, a prostate-specific GPCR (Vanti et al., 2003; Regard et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites published studies (Vanti et al., 2003; Regard et al., 2008) that characterized GPR137 expression.

claim: GPR137 is most closely related to OR51E2/PSGR, a prostate-specific GPCR.
source: GPR137 is ubiquitously and abundantly expressed in mouse tissues and is most closely related to OR51E2/PSGR, a prostate-specific GPCR (Vanti et al., 2003; Regard et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites published studies (Vanti et al., 2003; Regard et al., 2008) that identified this relationship.

claim: Silencing of GPR137 resulted in a downregulation of SNAI1/SNAIL and SNAI2/SLUG in human prostate cancer cells.
source: Indeed, silencing of GPR137 resulted in a downregulation of SNAI1/SNAIL and SNAI2/SLUG and a corresponding increase in E-cadherin expression in human prostate cancer cells (Ren et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study (Ren et al., 2016) that showed this effect of GPR137 silencing.

claim: Silencing of GPR137 resulted in a corresponding increase in E-cadherin expression in human prostate cancer cells.
source: Indeed, silencing of GPR137 resulted in a downregulation of SNAI1/SNAIL and SNAI2/SLUG and a corresponding increase in E-cadherin expression in human prostate cancer cells (Ren et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study (Ren et al., 2016) that showed this effect of GPR137 silencing.

claim: Gpr137_Short and hGPR137_Short are predicted to encode a protein with five transmembrane domains.
source: Gpr137_Short and hGPR137_Short are predicted to encode a protein with five transmembrane domains, whereas the products of Gpr137_Long and hGPR137_Long have a seven-transmembrane-spanning motif.

claim: The products of Gpr137_Long and hGPR137_Long have a seven-transmembrane-spanning motif.
source: Gpr137_Short and hGPR137_Short are predicted to encode a protein with five transmembrane domains, whereas the products of Gpr137_Long and hGPR137_Long have a seven-transmembrane-spanning motif.
evidence: Structural prediction based on sequence analysis.

claim: Human and mouse GPR137 proteins have a 78% identity.
source: Human and mouse GPR137 proteins have a 78% identity, yet the respective short and long isoforms we report here do not directly match between the two species.
evidence: Sequence comparison analysis reported in the text.

claim: The respective short and long GPR137 isoforms do not directly match between human and mouse.
source: Human and mouse GPR137 proteins have a 78% identity, yet the respective short and long isoforms we report here do not directly match between the two species.
evidence: Sequence comparison analysis reported in the text.

claim: The Wnt/β-catenin pathway is central to maintain tissue renewal and stem cell activity in IECs.
source: The Wnt/β-catenin pathway is central to maintain tissue renewal and stem cell activity in IECs as well as epithelial cell proliferation in intestinal crypts.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge of Wnt signaling in the intestine.

claim: Genetic ablation of β-catenin in adult mice leads to intestinal epithelial stem cell differentiation.
source: Genetic ablation of β-catenin in adult mice leads to intestinal epithelial stem cell (IESC) differentiation, thereby resulting in impaired intestinal homeostasis and fatal loss of intestinal function (Fevr et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study (Fevr et al., 2007) that showed this effect of β-catenin ablation.

claim: Genetic ablation of β-catenin in adult mice results in impaired intestinal homeostasis and fatal loss of intestinal function.
source: Genetic ablation of β-catenin in adult mice leads to intestinal epithelial stem cell (IESC) differentiation, thereby resulting in impaired intestinal homeostasis and fatal loss of intestinal function (Fevr et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study (Fevr et al., 2007) that showed this effect of β-catenin ablation.

claim: Reduced Wnt/β-catenin signaling likely underlies the diminished healing capacity of Triaka IECs.
source: Reduced Wnt/β-catenin signaling likely underlies the diminished healing capacity of Triaka IECs and their reduced proliferation after transformation in the AOM/DSS model.
evidence: Inference based on the wound-healing and tumor data combined with Wnt signaling measurements.

claim: Reduced Wnt/β-catenin signaling likely underlies the reduced proliferation of Triaka IECs after transformation in the AOM/DSS model.
source: Reduced Wnt/β-catenin signaling likely underlies the diminished healing capacity of Triaka IECs and their reduced proliferation after transformation in the AOM/DSS model.
evidence: Inference based on the tumor data combined with Wnt signaling measurements.

claim: CD44 and its isoforms negatively regulate IEC apoptosis.
source: CD44 and its isoforms negatively regulate IEC apoptosis (Zeilstra et al., 2008; Lakshman et al., 2004) and participate in various cellular functions, such as proliferation, adhesion, and migration (Ponta et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript cites published studies (Zeilstra et al., 2008; Lakshman et al., 2004) that showed this anti-apoptotic function.

claim: CD44 and its isoforms participate in various cellular functions, such as proliferation, adhesion, and migration.
source: CD44 and its isoforms negatively regulate IEC apoptosis (Zeilstra et al., 2008; Lakshman et al., 2004) and participate in various cellular functions, such as proliferation, adhesion, and migration (Ponta et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study (Ponta et al., 2003) that described these cellular functions.

claim: CD44v4 and CD44v6 isoforms are overexpressed in neoplastic IECs of patients with familial adenomatous polyposis.

claim: CD44 variant isoforms promote CRC in ApcMin/+ mice.
source: The expression of Cd44v4 and Cd44v6 isoforms in murine IESCs positively correlates with expression of LGR5, a marker of adult IESCs, and CD44 variant isoforms promote CRC in ApcMin/+ mice (Zeilstra et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study (Zeilstra et al., 2014) that showed this pro-tumorigenic function.

claim: ESRP1 may regulate the differentiation of adult stem cells, including IESCs.
source: ESRP1 has also been reported to restrict pluripotency in embryonic stem cells (Fagoonee et al., 2013), and it may as well regulate the differentiation of adult stem cells, including IESCs.

claim: EMT is associated with reduced proliferation of malignant cells.
source: As EMT is associated with reduced proliferation as well as increased motility and invasiveness of malignant cells, this may account for the phenotype of Triaka tumors (Kalluri and Weinberg, 2009; Evdokimova et al., 2009; Hur et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites published studies (Kalluri and Weinberg, 2009; Evdokimova et al., 2009; Hur et al., 2013) that described these features of EMT.

source: As EMT is associated with reduced proliferation as well as increased motility and invasiveness of malignant cells, this may account for the phenotype of Triaka tumors (Kalluri and Weinberg, 2009; Evdokimova et al., 2009; Hur et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites published studies (Kalluri and Weinberg, 2009; Evdokimova et al., 2009; Hur et al., 2013) that described these features of EMT.

source: Although we investigated ESRP1 expression and not ESRP1 mutations in human CRC, our in vitro data indicate a direct correlation between ESRP1 expression and splicing activity mediated by ESRP1.
